pr_body:
I'm sure there's a reason systemd has several different ways to determine the root device and that the current code covers many use cases that I haven't thought of. I tested this patch against 256.5 where it worked *for my use case*, so I figured I'd at least suggest it.

That disclaimer aside, below is the commit message:

systemd-sysupdate fails if `[Target]` has `Path=auto` and a sysext is in use.

```
root@localhost:~# /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-sysupdate list
Failed to find whole disk device for partition backing file system: No such device

root@localhost:~# mount | grep /usr
/dev/sda4 on /usr type ext4 (rw,relatime)
sysext on /usr type overlay (ro,relatime,lowerdir=/run/systemd/sysext/meta/usr:/run/systemd/sysext/extensions/SysExt_0/usr:/usr)
```

`bootctl -R` works correctly:

```
root@localhost:~# bootctl -R
/dev/nvme0n1p7
```

This change makes sd-sysupdate use the same function as `bootctl -R`.

Fixes #24562
pr_comments:
> LGTM.
> 
> Could you update the commit title ? `sysupdate: use blockdev_get_root()` That is, prefix with the component, and suffix function name with `()`.

Done.

Hmm, yeah, this is kinda broken. I guess we need to teach `systemd-sysext` to save the backing device of /usr/ to /run/systemd/volatile-usr or so, and then actually use that info in sysupdate before checking /run/systemd/volatile-root.

I am pretty sure /usr/ is the right thing to look at in general, not /. That is generally the right approach as long as we only issue stat() to find the backing device. But once we do the /run/systemd/volatile-xyz business we need to check explicitly for the user version, and then the rootfs version because the kernel is not going to do that for us like it would do for that stat() on /usr/ itself.

issue_context.title: Cannot run sysupdate if system extension images are in use
issue_context.body:
### systemd version the issue has been seen with

251

### Used distribution

Ubuntu Kinetic

### Linux kernel version used

5.15.0-27-generic

### CPU architectures issue was seen on

x86_64

### Component

systemd-sysext, other

### Expected behaviour you didn't see

If a system extension image is mounted then a command like `systemd-sysupdate list` should still work.

### Unexpected behaviour you saw

An error message as shown further below.

### Steps to reproduce the problem

1. Run `systemd-sysupdate list` without any system extension images to confirm proper configuration.
2. Mount a system extension image using `systemd-sysext merge`.
3. Run  `systemd-sysupdate list` again.

### Additional program output to the terminal or log subsystem illustrating the issue

```sh
# /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-sysupdate list
Failed to find whole disk device for partition backing file system: No such device

# mount | grep /usr
/dev/sda4 on /usr type ext4 (rw,relatime)
sysext on /usr type overlay (ro,relatime,lowerdir=/run/systemd/sysext/meta/usr:/run/systemd/sysext/extensions/SysExt_0/usr:/usr)

```
comments: A quick search over the code suggests that the overlay mount is causing `get_block_device_harder_fd()` defined under `src/shared/blockdev-util.c` to fail to find the backing block device.
@DaanDeMeyer @poettering This one is still an outstanding issue. Any update?

For GNOME OS we're working on integrating sysupdate with sysexts better, and we haven't run into this. Are you able to reproduce this still? Or was it something that got fixed at some point and the issue just remained open?
Sorry it has taken me this long to get back to you. It's still an issue under Ubuntu 24.04 (systemd v255.4).

I've hit this issue too.

@AdrianVovk Does GNOME OS happen to use a volatile root? I can work around the issue by creating `/run/systemd/volatile-root` as a symlink that points to the real device behind `/usr`.

That corresponds to:

https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/b45730389ba025489ec8d445bc91534fef515c28/src/sysupdate/sysupdate-resource.c#L586-L589

In my case `/usr` is part of my `/` which is an erofs. I have a sysext merged, so `/usr` is an overlayfs.

This is a somewhat customized Ubuntu 24.10 system with systemd 256.5 and vanilla (kernel.org) 6.11 kernel.

`bootctl -R` / `bootctl -RR` have the right idea:

```
root@localhost:~# /usr/lib/systemd/systemd-sysupdate
Failed to find whole disk device for partition backing file system: No such device
root@localhost:~# bootctl -R
/dev/nvme0n1p7
root@localhost:~# bootctl -RR
/dev/nvme0n1
```

Could they be made to use the same logic?

If nothing else that code from `src/sysupdate/sysupdate-resource.c` looks to be somewhat duplicated with https://github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/0d879453acdc86b0d742c5854420c116d0f23ba4/src/shared/blockdev-util.c#L867-L876 but the shared code also looks for whatever backs `/`. I've seen a mix:

* cryptenroll searches for `/var` and has a documented justification for `/var` which makes a lot of sense
* repart searches for `/` and `/usr`
* bootctl and gpt-auto-generator rely on `blockdev_get_root()` which is what is shown above

I'm sure there are other code snippets around that also look for the backing device of root. My quick search suggests that some refactoring might be needed.

review_comments:
The comment below explicitly states why the current form is preferred. At the minimum it needs to be dropped.

But I doubt it's the right approach at all. With this suddenly /usr/ is not considered the "closure" of system resource anymore.

Good catch on the comment. I'll get rid of it.

Looking *only* at `/usr` in an attempt to learn what the *root* device is seems suspect on its face and is exactly why this doesn't work. When there's a sysext mounted/merged, `/usr` is an overlayfs. The comment even starts with "If the root mount has been replaced[...]", but... what if it hasn't? And what if `/usr` has?

blockdev_get_root() checks `/run/systemd/volatile-root` first, then `/`, then finally `/usr` which sounds exactly like the approach I would have expected to find in resource_resolve_path() based on the comment. 

What's the logic behind only looking at `/usr` and *completely ignoring* `/` when the objective is to learn what block device is backing `/`?

Hmm. Rereading the comment in the comment, I think we cannot `blockdev_get_root()` here.
Maybe, better to introduce `blockdev_get_usr()` or so, which does something similar to `blockdev_get_root()`, but searching `/usr/`, and gracefully handle sysext.

Look, the docs say:

> If Type= is set to partition, expects a path to a (whole) block device node, or the special string "auto" in which case the block device which contains the root file system of the currently booted system is automatically determined and used.

Why this obsession with `/usr`? It doesn't even have to be on the same disk as `/`.

Honestly, this is beginning to feel gaslighty. The docs are clear. They don't mention `/usr` at all. The reported issue is caused exactly by the fact that even though the objective ostensibly is to determine the root device, you want to ignore the root device entirely, because sometimes it doesn't work, because it's masked by a tmpfs or whatever... but when `/usr` is masked BY A PART OF SYSTEMD, there's no fall back.

If this is truly how it's supposed to (not) work, I'll change the patch to a docs change that says that Path=auto doesn't work when a sysext is in use. I'm at a loss as to whose benefit this for, but better to at least have the docs and the behavior agree.
